CI phases

scripts/ci.mjs

In call order, read out of main(). A fast phase also runs on --fast and in the pre-push hook; the rest only on a full run.

01
hygienefast

Everything here is about the difference between THIS working copy and a fresh clone.

02
structurefast

The architecture rules, run over this repo's own apps and packages with the same engine `fli check` gives a client app.

03
registersfast

The three registers, graded against the rules they state about themselves.

04
snapshotsfast

A snapshot is a generated artefact committed beside its source, so a change nothing else in the repo can see arrives as a diff: the access rules enforced below the API, the DDL every hand-written statement binds to, the JSON Schema three packages validate…

05
accessfast

What did this branch do to who may do what.

06
coveragefast

Skipped is not passed. The aggregate `--filter '*'` walks straight past a package with no `test` script and prints nothing at all about it.

07
registryfast
08
advisoriesfast

Dependency posture, decided the way everything else here is decided: a phase, not a bot (`IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md` 5).

09
scaffoldfast
10
typecheckfast

Two halves: the direction of the ratchet (a git question) and the count itself (each package's own script already answers that, and exits 1 above its ceiling).

11
deployfull run

`fli new` → `fli make:deploy` → `fli deploy:local`: does the deploy pipeline containerize a real app? ~30s and it needs a Docker daemon, so it sits in the full tier rather than the pre-push one.

12
tutorfull run

The tutorial, executed. `docs/QUICKSTART.md` §7 exited 0 on every command it named and had never once put an app on a server — a document with no compiler behind it, which is the failure every other phase here exists to prevent one realm at a time. A lesson is…

13
testsfull run

Sequential on purpose: several suites bind ports and start real servers, and interleaved output from four different runners is unreadable when one fails.

API design (Junction) 70 FJS-D338 How a per-call value too big for a header reaches the boundary — a header-flagged body envelope: X-Fjs-Write: enveloped and a body of { data, base }, with the header absent meaning today's plain-data…

Design system (`@frontierjs/css`) 18 FJS-D252 Bar is the strip and Group is what goes inside it.

Which drive proves a change

132 rows · 220 targets · 1 not found

Parsed from DRIVES.md, never restated. The third column is each target resolved against the tree — not found is a row naming a drive that has been renamed, which in the markdown reads exactly like a row that is right. Half these rows are not import edges: a gate on a model a screen reads is a statement about what a drive can SEE, so this is a parse and not a build graph.

The engine is litestone's and is proved by packages/litestone: bun run test:browser, which is the only thing that runs it over OPFS at all. What NEITHER can see is the packaging, and the packaging is where this breaks: a bundler rewrites new Worker(new URL(…, import.meta.url)) and nothing else, the wasm entry must be served as .js, and that same static signal puts the worker in every app unless the build stubs it out — each of those failed silently, with the app looking like it worked. So a change here is also cd example && bun run build, read for the shell WEIGHT — and the numbers are three, not one: 1 kB is the seam in an app that left the database off, 880 kB is example with it on, and anything near 400 means the worker is being shipped by an app that did not ask for it (FJS-D302). example: verify:shell is what grades the feature end to end, and its decisive block is the one that empties the list cache with the network already down and asks the screen again: every other assertion passes with the database absent, because a slot a load() wrote answers the same question with the same rows. Since FJS-D337 the WARM writes no such slot for a model the device kept, which the drive asserts directly. That is how orderBy: '-id' reaching SQLite unchanged — junction's wire spelling, which litestone throws on — was invisible for as long as it existed packages/sierratest/local-db.test.jspackages/litestonebun run test:browserexampleverify:shell
the DECLARED OFFLINE READ — sierra/src/junction/offline.js, offlineQuery, or anything that builds a cache key packages/sierra: test/offline-query.test.js. Every case is warmed, then offline, then read and never the warm ran, because the way this feature fails is a warm written under a key no load() looks under — which nothing about the app looks wrong for until somebody is in a basement. Two negative controls keep that honest: breaking the key turns 6 of the 13 red, and routing the warm through load() instead of find() turns exactly the the store the screen is showing is not touched case red. A change to listKey, to either side of the warm, or to when it is armed needs a case here. The warm also fills the DEVICE's tables, which is hydration, and that half is graded in test/local-db.test.js under a question the warm never asked — the only kind a cache cannot answer. Its fake device KEEPS what it is given, because one that answers reads regardless cannot tell a hydrated device from an empty one, and the sharpest test here passed against a device nothing had written to until it did. example: verify:shell is the end of it — a screen opened offline for the first time in that browser with the cache emptied, and since FJS-D337 with no slot for the warm to have written at all: what the drive waits on is the warm's own frame, tapped before the app's first script, because a fact nothing writes cannot be read back · verify:offline for the queue underneath it packages/sierratest/offline-query.test.jsexampleverify:shell
the SCHEMA A DEVICE GETS — src/device-schema.js, or a parser change adding a node kind a model can reach packages/litestone: test/device-schema.test.ts, and test:browser. The unit file is the pairings — what crosses beside what does not, since a filter that kept everything passes every test asserting only presence — and its last four cases run over example's real 53-model schema, because a construct a fixture does not have is exactly what a filter drops by accident. Both ends hand the output to createClient and write a row through it, through a JSON round trip: a filter over a tree is the kind of code that looks right in a snapshot and produces something no client can open. A new node kind reachable from a field (an enum, a type, a value set) needs a case here or it arrives on a device as a name nothing defines packages/litestonetest/device-schema.test.ts

Both are needed and neither subsumes the other: the node fixture cannot see a browser, and the browser drive cannot be run from a bun test — and neither could see the third thing in that file, a static walk of the browser entries' import graph refusing a bare node builtin, because node has fs under every condition and only a BUNDLER replaces it with something that throws on the first property access (FJS-1179) packages/litestonetest/engine-seam.test.ts

The two that have to stay are the JSON.stringify row, which is why the value crosses as digits rather than as a BigInt and covers every response, frame and audit snapshot in one line; and count() answering a number, because safeIntegers is per-statement and all-or-nothing, so a count is the shape that escapes a narrowing done in the row read. test/import.test.ts is the other half — a foreign BIGINT is CARRIED now, and what it emits has to parse packages/litestonetest/big-int.test.ts

The negative controls are the test: a predicate SQLite cannot prove at prepare time is not a slower index, it is an unused one. example is the end-to-end half — ProductVariant declares the repo's only where:, so a real app's parse, migration and ddl.snapshot.sql cross it, and verify:catalog reads the variant grid through it packages/litestonetest/index-predicates.test.ts
a partial unique — @@unique([cols], where: …), partialUnique, the predicate in release.js packages/litestone: test/index-predicates.test.ts — the same file as the two rows below and a third reader. The assertions that have to stay are the ones the design turns on: the soft-delete clause is ABSENT from the emitted DDL, asserted against the text because the constraint behaves identically either way until a row is deleted; a value comparison is INLINED, because SQLite refuses a bound parameter there and every behavioral test passes against DDL that never built; it does not make a relation one-to-one; and the RENAME — a database written before the uniq<table><cols> prefix carries the index under the old name, and leaving it there makes the model's own @@index over those columns a CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS against a name already taken, which SQLite answers by doing nothing (FJS-614). The control beside it is a hand-made index of the same shape, which must NOT be renamed or duplicated. example: verify:employment is the end-to-end half and the only place a second open window is attempted against a real database — through asSystem() AND through a raw INSERT, which is what separates a table rule from a boundary one packages/litestonetest/index-predicates.test.tsexampleverify:employment
